title: How Will the Moon Decide When Ramadan 2027 Begins?
question: How will the moon decide when Ramadan 2027 begins, and why does a one-day difference matter for prices, travel and budgets around the world?
description: UAE astronomers say Ramadan 2027 is expected to begin on Monday 8 February, but this February the same holy month began on two different days in different countries. We explain how a thin crescent moon sets the date, why sighting, calculation and national rules can disagree, and how the calendar moves food prices, working hours and flights from Jakarta to Cairo to Dubai. We also set out what could happen in the first week of February 2027 and some calm ways to plan ahead. Should the world share one calculated date, or should each country sight its own moon? Tell us in the comments.

ad_safety.reason: Educational explainer on a calendar, astronomy and seasonal economics, handled respectfully with no conflict, violence or divisive politics.

scenes.narration: UAE astronomers say Ramadan 2027 is expected to begin on Monday, 8 February. The important word in that sentence is expected.

That forecast, which UAE media have reported since late summer and repeated in October, rests on astronomical calculations. The official start still waits until authorities confirm the new crescent moon.

visual.text: UAE astronomers say Ramadan 2027 expected to begin on February 8

scenes.narration: This February, the same holy month began on two different days. Saudi Arabia announced Wednesday 18 February, while Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore announced Thursday 19 February.
So how will the moon decide when Ramadan 2027 begins, and why does a single day matter for food prices, flights and your budget?
First, the clock. The Islamic calendar follows the Moon, and each month begins with the first thin crescent, called the hilal, seen after sunset.
That crescent appears low in the western sky, and atmospheric conditions can hide it, which is one reason two countries can reach different answers.
An Islamic year lasts 354 or 355 days, about 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan arrives earlier in the seasons every year.
If you want one big story explained like this every day, subscribe. Now, how does a month actually begin?
The Moon takes about 29 and a half days to complete its cycle of phases, so a month lasts 29 or 30 days, never 31, and the sky decides which.

Some communities sight locally, some follow another country, and others calculate. In 2007, the European Council for Fatwa and Research ruled calculation a permissible way to fix the start of lunar months, including Ramadan.

visual.heading: Three ways to start a month

scenes.narration: The new Moon itself is invisible. A day or so later the crescent may show after sunset, and a committee reviews reports and announces the date.
Most countries with large Muslim populations have an official body for this, often scholars working with astronomers. In Saudi Arabia, any Muslim can report a sighting to the authorities.

Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore share a rule: the crescent must be at least 3 degrees high and 6.4 degrees from the Sun. On 17 February, it was below the horizon across Indonesia at sunset, far short of the 3-degree requirement.

UK astronomy forecasts, including those published with the Royal Observatory Greenwich, showed the crescent would not be visible on 17 February. Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court nonetheless accepted reports that the crescent had been sighted and declared 18 February.

visual.text: Saudi Arabia declares Ramadan 2026 start date despite 'not visible' moon warning

scenes.narration: In Jakarta, the Religious Affairs Ministry held a confirmation meeting, called an isbat. The crescent did not meet its rule, so fasting began on Thursday 19 February.

visual.text: Indonesian government declares Feb 19 as start of Ramadan

scenes.narration: Even inside Indonesia there was a split. The Muhammadiyah organisation began on 18 February, while the government and Nahdlatul Ulama began on 19 February, using different methods.
Reports indicate most Gulf states began on 18 February, while Indonesia, Singapore and many European and Asian communities began on 19 February.
Now the scenario. None of this has happened yet. It shows how the first week of February 2027 could unfold.

visual.text: Now the scenario / Not yet happened

scenes.narration: The International Astronomical Centre places the new Moon on Saturday 6 February at 15:56 UTC, after UAE sunset. The crescent is not expected to be visible then, so Shaban would run 30 days and fasting could begin Monday 8 February.

visual.title: How the date could be set

scenes.narration: In the UAE, official moon sighting still confirms the final date, and astronomers expect Monday 8 February. Countries relying on calculation or their own criteria could land on a different day.
If 2026 is any guide, a one-day gap could open again between the Gulf, Southeast Asia and Europe, each following its own method. The forecasts do not say that it will.
Ramadan would then last 29 or 30 days. That puts Eid al-Fitr on Tuesday 9 March or Wednesday 10 March, depending on the crescent at the end of the month.

In the UAE, the Eid holiday covers at least the first three days of Shawwal, and the announced break can start earlier, on 29 Ramadan in some years. A one-day shift in the crescent can therefore move the whole break.
Now your money. None of this is a prediction, and none of it is financial advice. But Ramadan reliably changes spending, so the date matters to household budgets.

visual.sub: What the calendar does to prices

scenes.narration: Indonesia's March 2025 monthly inflation hit 1.65 percent as Ramadan began, but most of that came from the end of a temporary electricity discount rather than Ramadan demand.

Market estimates cited by Arab Finance put Egypt's total monthly spending at around 100 billion pounds in Ramadan, against roughly 55 billion in an average month, with higher spending on food, hospitality and gifts.
Dates are a signature food for breaking the fast. Indonesia's agriculture ministry says consumption typically surges by as much as 50 percent during the month.
Working hours change too. Onshore in the UAE, the day is cut by two hours, and in Saudi Arabia Muslim employees are limited to six hours a day.
Some travel sites report that fares can be lower during Ramadan and rise before Eid, but this varies by route and year.
Some households plan ahead for the food price bump and look for flexible tickets, since the Eid date could shift by a day.
So the moon decides in steps: astronomers forecast, observers look, and an authority rules. The forecast gives planners a date, but only the ruling makes it official.

Back to that word, expected. This February, Riyadh and many Jakarta families began fasting a day apart: Saudi Arabia accepted a sighting report UK forecasts said was not visible, while Indonesia's government found the crescent below its thresholds.
Which would you prefer: one shared date set by calculation, or each country sighting its own moon? Tell us in the comments.

factcheck.summary: Almost all dates, figures and timelines check out (the 8 Feb 2027 forecast, the 15:56 UTC new moon, the Feb 2026 Saudi and Indonesian decisions, MABIMS 3°/6.4°, the 1.65% inflation, the EGP 100bn and 55bn estimates, and the working-hours rules). Three wording or attribution fixes are needed: the cause of the split in scene 6, the unsupported Saudi claim in scene 12, and the date-consumption attribution in scene 27. There are no advertiser-friendliness problems.

open_issues.claim: That crescent appears low in the western sky, and atmospheric conditions can hide it, which is one reason two countries can reach different answers.
open_issues.problem: This misleads about the 2026 split, which the narration describes in later scenes. On 17 Feb 2026 the crescent was astronomically too young to see anywhere, and Indonesia's government put it below the horizon. The split came from different rules: Saudi Arabia accepted a sighting report, while others applied calculation-based visibility criteria. Weather was not the cause. Atmosphere does affect visibility in general.
open_issues.fix: That crescent is thin and low in the western sky, and it is hard to see. Countries can reach different answers because they use different rules: some accept sighting reports, some use calculated visibility criteria, and some follow another country.

open_issues.claim: In Saudi Arabia, any Muslim can report a sighting to the authorities.
open_issues.problem: None of the sources checked support this. They describe observer teams and committees filing reports to the Supreme Court, which then rules on them. The narration also implies anyone's report is accepted, but the court validates witness testimony.
open_issues.fix: In Saudi Arabia, observer teams across the country report sightings to the Supreme Court, which validates the testimony and announces the date. (Or remove the 'any Muslim' claim unless a Saudi Supreme Court source is added.)

open_issues.claim: Indonesia's agriculture ministry says consumption typically surges by as much as 50 percent during the month.
open_issues.problem: The figure comes from one named official, a director of downstream plantation products at the Ministry of Agriculture, as quoted by The Straits Times. It is not an official ministry statement.
open_issues.fix: An Indonesian Agriculture Ministry official says date consumption typically surges by as much as 50 percent during the fasting month.

strengths: The Feb 2026 Saudi vs Indonesia split is a real, checkable 'wait, really?' fact: Saudi Arabia accepted a sighting that UK forecasts called 'not visible', while Indonesia's own rule was missed.
Scenario and fact are clearly flagged ('None of this has happened yet', 'The forecasts do not say that it will').
The ladder and timeline visuals for the 8 Feb date and the 9/10 March Eid are clean and match their lines.
Money is calm, carries no stock tips, and hedges honestly ('varies by route and year').
The closing question (shared calculated date vs national sighting) is a genuine debate that invites comments.
problems: Question: a forecast for a date 4+ months away is not 'the big story people are talking about today'. The 'what happens if' is weak because the answer is only that the date may be off by a day. A viewer in Lagos has no stake until the episode shows what a one-day gap costs.

Hook: it opens on a dry forecast ('expected'), and the real surprise (two start dates in one month) only arrives in scene 3. The question lands in scene 4, likely past 20 seconds. The headline is dated 11 Oct 2026 yet the narration says 'this February', which muddles the timeline.

Story: the first half is an explainer and a recap of 2026 before the scenario starts. The scenario is mostly one ladder and a timeline. The stakes never rise from place to region to world. There is no moment where a family, a shop or a flight is affected.

Surprise: the facts are not sourced on screen or in narration, and the 30-link list gives no way to see which source backs which claim. Two of the best facts are buried: the crescent was below the horizon across Indonesia, and Indonesia itself split between 18 and 19 Feb. The 29/30-day and 354-day facts are not surprising.

Clarity: there are no real analogies. The terms isbat, Shaban, hilal and 'MABIMS rule' are unexplained or dropped in. '3 degrees high and 6.4 degrees from the Sun' is opaque to a 12-year-old. Scene 6's atmospheric explanation is factually wrong for 2026 and confuses the mechanism.

Money: the Indonesia 1.65% inflation scene undercuts itself, since the narration says it was mostly an electricity discount ending. Egypt's 100bn EGP is a national total, not a household number. The flights segment is vague. 'Calm moves' is two bullet points with no numbers or actions. Nothing is useful to a worker, freelancer or small shop owner anywhere. It is Muslim-world-centric with no jobs, savings or rates angle.

Visuals: the Gulf close-up map is generic and adds nothing to a line about committees and sighting. The 1.65% stat shows a number the narration disowns. The dates photo and the crescent photo carry no news weight. Maps are used for explanation where paper scenes would fit better.

Accuracy: the factcheck is ok:false with three open issues. Scene 6 wrongly implies atmosphere caused the split. Scene 12's 'any Muslim can report a sighting' in Saudi Arabia is unsupported. Scene 27's 'agriculture ministry says' is really one official. The wording 'Saudi accepted a report UK forecasts said was not visible' reads slightly like a verdict and should be neutral. The 2007 ECFR claim is cited to a page whose URL says 2020.
